fireprime_intro: FIREPRIME is an app that helps you self-assess the wildfire risk of your home.You can carry out two types of assessment: a basic one and an advanced one, and also access key preparedness and safety advice.
instructions_intro: To get started, enter your home's location.
notification_body: It's been a year since you completed the wildfire risk self-assessment. Take the questionnaire again to see if the improvements you've made have reduced your home's vulnerability.
about_intro: Wildfire risk self-assessment at the parcel level

questionnaire_intro:
· The questionnaire consists of 23 questions with multiple answer options. Unless otherwise indicated, you should select only one. 
· It includes images and explanations to help you understand some technical concepts. 
· If in doubt, choose the option that best describes your situation. 
· Take your time: it may take up to 30 minutes, as you’ll need to carefully observe the façade and surroundings of your home. You can complete it at different times. 
· Answer based on the condition of your home during the months of highest wildfire risk. 
·It is recommended to repeat the assessment at least once a year or after significant changes to the house or its surroundings. 
·The questionnaire is divided into two parts: building and surroundings.
basic_questionnaire_intro:
Assess the vulnerability of your home by answering Yes or No to a 10-question survey. 
If in doubt, choose the option that best represents your situation.

I1.title: Questions about the building
I1.text: The construction elements and materials of buildings located in the wildland-urban interface may have weak points that allow fire to enter. In this first section, you should inspect the entire building envelope to identify these vulnerabilities.

Q1.title: Facade materials
Q1.question: What percentage of the facade (exterior walls and balconies, excluding shutters, windows and porches) is made of combustible materials?
Q1.description: Wood or facade covering materials made from plastics or polymers are combustible while concrete, stone or bricks are non-combustible, fire-resistant.
Q1.more50comb: More than or equal to 50% combustible

Q2.title: Facade materials
Q2.question: Is the combustible part of the facade adjacent to the ground?
Q2.description: If the combustible part of the facade is adjacent to the ground, it will be more likely to ignite if fire reaches it.
Q2.height0to20: No, the fuel part is at a height between 0 and 20 cm from the ground
Q2.height21to40: No, the fuel part is between 21 and 40 cm above the ground
Q2.height41to60: No, the fuel part is between 41 and 60 cm above the ground
Q2.height61to80: No, the fuel part is between 61 and 80 cm above the ground
Q2.height81to100: No, the combustible part is at a height between 81 cm and 1 m from the ground
Q2.heightMore100: No, the fuel part is at a height greater than 1 m

Q3.title: Roof
Q3.question: Is the roof covered with fire-resistant materials (ceramic tiles, concrete tiles, slate tiles, etc.)?
Q3.description: If you have solar panels on the roof, this question refers to the material on which they are installed.
Q3.roofNonFireRated: No, the roof is covered with combustible materials (wood, asphalt shingles, etc.)

Q4-1.title: Roof
Q4-1.question: Does the roof have any of the following characteristics? Broken or missing shingles, exposed insulation, or unsealed spaces between the roof and the facade.
Q4-1.description: A roof in poor condition can allow embers from fire smoke to pass through and cause a fire inside the house.

Q4-2.title: Roof
Q4-2.question: Does the roof have any of the following characteristics? Broken or missing shingles, exposed insulation, or unsealed spaces between the roof and the facade.
Q4-2.description: A roof in poor condition can allow embers from fire smoke to pass through and cause a fire inside the house.

Q5.title: Glazing systems
Q5.question: What is the most common type of glass in building enclosures?
Q5.description: Glass is a material vulnerable to fire. One way to improve its resistance is to use glass made up of several sheets (double or triple glazing) or with special treatments (such as tempered glass). If your building has more than one type of glass enclosure, select the most representative one.

Q6.title: Glazing systems
Q6.question: Are glass enclosures protected with shutters? If so, what is the most common material for shutters (choose the option that best describes your situation)?
Q6.description: Blinds can protect windows from the effects of fire. It should be noted that to block the heat emitted by a fire, blinds and their slats must be completely closed.

Q7.title: Ventilations
Q7.question: What kind of protection do the ventilation openings have?
Q7.description: Ventilations are openings located in the roof or in the kitchen, designed to facilitate ventilation of interior spaces. If you have more than one (protected or not), choose the answer that best represents your case.
Q7.nonCombGoodCond: The protection is non-combustible and in good condition
Q7.nonCombBadCond: The protection is non-combustible but is in poor condition (rusted or broken)

Q8.title: Semi-open spaces adjacent to the building
Q8.question: Are there any semi-open spaces adjacent to the building (with at least one wall in common), such as porches, sheds, or spaces under terraces, that contain combustible objects inside?
Q8.description: Semi-open spaces are partially covered areas, adjacent to the building, such as porches, spaces under terraces, awnings or sheds, where combustible elements (furniture, wood, etc.) often accumulate. If fire reaches them, the accumulation of heat can be significant.

Q9.title: Glass enclosures in semi-open spaces
Q9.question: Are there any unprotected glass enclosures (such as windows or doors) that connect the semi-open space with the interior of the building?
Q9.description: In the event of a fire, unprotected glass in semi-open spaces can break if the fire affects materials stored in these spaces.
Q9.glazingSystemsMultiplePane: Yes, with double or triple glazing

Q10.title: Walls of the semi-open space
Q10.question: What material is the exterior of the building facade that borders the semi-open space made of?
Q10.description:
In the event of a fire, unprotected glass in semi-open spaces can break if the fire affects the materials stored in these spaces. 
Wood or plastic cladding are combustible materials that, in the event of a fire in the semi-open space, can facilitate the entry of fire into the house.
Q10.combustibleEnvelope: Combustible material such as wood or plastic cladding
Q10.nonCombThin: Non-combustible material such as steel or aluminum
Q10.nonCombThick: Non-combustible materials such as bricks or concrete

I2.title: Questions about the environment
I2.text: Combustible elements near the building are those that can catch fire during a wildfire. Examples of natural combustible elements include cypress hedges, dry grass, shrubs, trees, etc. Lawns or green grass are not considered combustible. Examples of non-natural combustible elements include garden furniture, tool or animal sheds, pergolas, wooden decking, outbuildings, vehicles, etc. Additionally, the slope of the terrain and the proximity to the forest are also key factors that influence the fire risk of the property.

Q11.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q11.question: Identify what combustible elements you have near the building. Which of the following options apply?
Q11.description: Combustible elements (natural and unnatural) located near the building can easily ignite in the event of a forest fire and transmit the fire to the home through vulnerable points, such as unprotected glass or combustible components of the building.
Q11.5closeToGlazing: There are combustible elements placed less than 5 meters from enclosures with glass that are not protected by shutters.
Q11.closeToRoof: There are combustible elements within 5 meters of adjacent combustible elements on the roof (such as wooden eaves, PVC gutters for rainwater collection).
Q11.none: None of the options are applicable

Q12.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q12.question: Do you have combustible elements in direct contact with the facade? (if you have wooden flooring adjacent to a fully or partially combustible facade, take it into account in the analysis).
Q12.description: If there is a fire and embers reach it, combustible materials located next to a combustible facade can easily cause the fire to enter the house.

Q13.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q13.question: Do you have a continuous area of natural fuel (dry grass, young bushes, leaf litter) that reaches the facade? (if you have artificial grass, take it into account in the analysis).
Q13.description: An example of a continuous combustible surface is a garden with dry grass. Green grass or lawn is not combustible.

Q14.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q14.question: Are there combustible elements (natural or unnatural), located less than 2 meters from a hydrocarbon tank (LPG, diesel or gas cylinders with a volume greater than 0.5 m3)?
Q14.description: If there is a fire and embers reach it, combustible materials located near a hydrocarbon tank can put the tank at risk and cause a firestorm.

Q15.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q15.question: Identify what non-natural combustible elements you have near the building (garden furniture, tool or animal sheds, pergolas, sheds, cars, etc.). Which of the following options apply?
Q15.description: In the event of a fire, non-natural combustible materials can ignite and spread the fire to the building if they are too close.
Q15.placedIn20: There are unnatural combustible elements located less than 20 meters from an area with highly flammable vegetation (e.g. very dense scrub, wooded areas with species such as pines, eucalyptus, cypresses, etc.).
Q15.spacingLess5: There is no minimum 5-meter spacing between non-natural combustible elements.
Q15.none: None of the options are applicable

Q16.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q16.question: Is the building located within 30 meters of a forest area (e.g. do you consider pasture, scrub or forest areas as forest areas)?
Q16.description: A forest area refers to a continuous area of pasture, scrub or forest of a certain extent. Unbuilt plots adjacent to the building, where vegetation has grown, should also be taken into account in the analysis.

Q17.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q17.question: Look at the trees and shrubs within a 30-meter radius around the building. What type of vegetation predominates there?
Q17.description: The degree of flammability of plant species determines how the fire will behave. Species such as pines or eucalyptus generate larger and more intense flames, while fruit trees, which are less flammable, burn with smaller flames.
Q17.mediumFlam: Moderately flammable (holm oak, mastic, oak, etc.)
Q17.noVeg: Not applicable (there are no trees or shrubs within a 30 meter radius around the building)

Q18.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q18.question: Look at the trees and shrubs within a 30-meter radius around the building. Is there horizontal continuity between them?
Q18.description: Horizontal continuity refers to the presence of vegetation connected or very close together in the horizontal plane, without empty spaces between the different elements. This arrangement makes it easier for fire to spread quickly from one point to another on the ground surface or at low altitude.
Q18.noApplicableDiscVeg: Not applicable (there are no trees or shrubs within a 30 meter radius around the building)

Q19.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q19.question: Look at the trees and shrubs within a 30-meter radius around the building. Is there vertical continuity between them?
Q19.description: Vertical vegetation continuity is the connection between different layers of vegetation—such as grass, shrubs, and trees—that form a kind of natural "staircase". This arrangement makes it easier for fire to spread from the ground to the canopy, making the fire more intense and difficult to control.
Q19.noApplicablePruning: Not applicable (there are no trees or shrubs within a 30 meter radius around the building)

Q20.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q20.question: How high is the continuous area of natural fuel (dry grass, young bushes, leaf litter) surrounding the building?
Q20.description: If there is very tall dry grass, it can spread the fire quite intensely and easily reach the building.

Q21.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q21.question: Is there an accumulation of dead vegetation or vegetation debris (leaves, pruning debris) within 30 meters of the building?
Q21.description: The accumulation of dry or dead fuel can burn easily and contribute to the spread of fire into the building.

Q22.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q22.question: Analyze the boundary elements on your plot. What is the predominant boundary?
Q22.description: Fences made of combustible materials can facilitate the spread of fire into the building and between neighbors
Q22.hedgerowHigh: Hedgerow of highly flammable shrubs (cypress, heather, etc.)
Q22.hedgerowLow: Hedgerow of low-flammable shrubs (laurel, cherry, etc.)
Q22.concreteMore2: Brick or metal fence or wall (with a minimum height of 2 meters)
Q22.concreteLess2: Concrete or metal fence/wall (less than 2 meters high)
Q22.noDelimitation: There is no fence or physical separation

Q23.title: Characteristics of the building environment
Q23.question: What type of terrain is your plot of land in?
Q23.description: Houses located mid-slope or on a ridge are more vulnerable, as the fire intensifies as it moves up the slope.
